authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant

items.prompt: A static array receives exactly one range-sum query, the requested range may cover most of the array, and extra memory should be minimized. Which strategy best matches this query volume?
constraints: Exactly one range-sum query will occur.
The array is static.
Extra memory should be minimized.

options.text: Scan the requested range once and accumulate the sum.
Build an O(n)-space prefix array, answer the one query, then discard it.
Sort the values before adding the requested range.

feedback.reason: With one query, a full prefix index has no repeated-query work to amortize and consumes O(n) extra space. A direct range scan satisfies the contract with minimal setup.

blocks.text: Query volume changes the lifecycle calculation. For one range, direct scanning costs O(length of range) and O(1) extra space. Building prefix sums costs O(n) time and O(n) space before a single O(1) query, so it offers no asymptotic total-time advantage when the range can be n and can perform more work for a short range. Sorting is illegal for positional range semantics and adds unrelated cost. The transfer rule is to prefer low-setup direct work when a reusable index will not be reused, unless latency or another explicit constraint requires preprocessing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_once: Prefix sums are correct, but their setup and O(n) state are not amortized by one query. They become preferable when many later queries reuse the same static prefix array or when a strict per-query latency requirement justifies setup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_first: Sorting changes which values occupy the requested indices and therefore violates range semantics. It would be relevant only for an order-insensitive query whose mechanism needs sorted values.

items.prompt: A static array of n values must answer q = 1,000,000 arbitrary inclusive range-sum queries [l, r], each of which may cover Θ(n) positions. Which strategy gives the best worst-case total time under the stated resources?
constraints: q is one million.
The array is unchanged between queries.
Queries ask additive ranges.
Each query may span a linear-size range.
O(n) extra memory is available.

options.text: Build prefix sums once in O(n), retain the O(n) cumulative array, and answer each of the one million range queries in O(1).
Scan every requested range independently so no preprocessing state is stored, even though the same array serves one million queries.
Before each query, sort the array and then add the values whose sorted positions fall between l and r.

feedback.reason: The static prefix state is reusable across all one million queries. Its O(n) setup is amortized while per-query work drops to O(1).

blocks.text: Define P[0] = 0 and build P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i] once. Every inclusive query [l, r] then returns P[r + 1] − P[l] in O(1) time, giving O(n + q) total time and O(n) extra space. Rescanning costs O(r − l + 1) per query and reaches O(nq) when the ranges are linear-sized. The array never changes, so the prefix index remains valid. Sorting changes positional range semantics and does not provide the required cancellation. The transfer rule is to invest in reusable preprocessing when the same data supports many compatible queries and the index remains valid for their entire lifetime.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rescan_each: A scan is attractive for one query, but repeating it up to a million times multiplies the data work by q. It becomes competitive when q is very small, ranges are tiny, or memory forbids the index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_each: Sorting changes positional range semantics and repeating it compounds the cost. Sorting can help repeated order-based queries only when performed once and when the output contract is compatible with reordered data.

items.prompt: A catalog of n immutable identifiers must answer many exact membership queries. Which workload-aware strategy is strongest when O(n) extra memory is acceptable and expected-time hash guarantees satisfy the contract?
constraints: Identifiers do not change.
There are many exact membership queries.
O(n) extra memory is available.
Expected-time hash guarantees are acceptable.

options.text: Scan all n identifiers for every membership request so the service avoids building and retaining any auxiliary lookup index.
Build one O(n)-space hash set in expected O(n) time, then reuse it for expected O(1) membership answers across the full query workload.
For each request, copy and sort the catalog, then binary-search the requested identifier in that newly ordered copy.

feedback.reason: Many queries can reuse one membership index. The setup cost is paid once rather than repeating a full scan.

blocks.text: A hash set changes the lifecycle from O(qn) repeated scans to expected O(n + q) operations with O(n) extra state. The exact output is membership, so no ordering or original-position witness is required. A one-time sorted index could also be a legal candidate with O(n log n + q log n), but sorting a fresh copy per query discards reuse. The transfer rule is to align the preprocessed state with the query primitive—membership, rank, range aggregate, predecessor, or nearest relation—and reuse it across the workload.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_catalog: Scanning avoids setup and can be best for one or very few queries, but repeated full passes make total work grow with qn. It becomes preferable when q is small or memory is too constrained for an index.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_per_query: This repeats the most expensive setup instead of reusing it. A single sorted copy could be considered when deterministic bounds or ordered queries matter.

items.prompt: The complete dataset is loaded before service starts. Queries then arrive online one at a time and require immediate answers, but the dataset remains unchanged. Which interpretation of query timing is correct?
constraints: All data is available before the first query.
Queries arrive later and are not known in advance.
The data remains static.

options.text: Preprocessing may be completed before service starts, then the stable index can answer online queries.
Online query arrival forbids all preprocessing.
The index must be rebuilt before every online query because the query was not known in advance.

feedback.reason: Online query arrival does not forbid preprocessing when the data is already complete and stable. It only prevents preprocessing that depends on future query contents.

blocks.text: Two timelines matter: when the data becomes available and when each answer is due. Here the dataset can be indexed during startup, and that index remains valid while unknown future queries arrive. The system cannot precompute each exact answer because query parameters are unknown, but it can precompute reusable structure such as a set, sorted copy, or prefix aggregates. Rebuilding per request would throw away the amortization benefit. The transfer rule is to separate data-offline/query-online workloads from true streaming-data workloads.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_preprocessing: This confuses unknown future queries with unavailable data. The claim becomes valid only when the dataset itself arrives online or preprocessing cannot finish before the first required answer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rebuild_each: A query-independent index is reusable even when query arguments are not known. Rebuilding is necessary only when intervening data updates invalidate the structure.

items.prompt: A range-sum workload alternates one point update with one query. The only proposed index is a plain prefix array that would be rebuilt in O(n) after every update. Which query-volume decision is justified?
constraints: Each query is preceded by a point update.
A plain prefix array requires a full rebuild.
No update-aware alternative is part of the candidate set.

options.text: Choose prefix sums because any repeated range query justifies preprocessing.
Build the prefix array once and answer from it even after values change.
Do not choose the prefix array merely because queries repeat; its O(n) rebuild removes the static-query advantage.

feedback.reason: Repeated queries justify preprocessing only when the preprocessed state remains reusable at acceptable maintenance cost. Alternating updates invalidate a plain prefix array.

blocks.text: The workload lifecycle is not q queries over one immutable snapshot. Under the stated maintenance policy, each update triggers O(n) work, so u updates and q queries cost O(un + q) after setup. That can be no better than direct rescanning for this balanced workload and uses additional state. Keeping the old prefix values would be incorrect. The transfer rule is to include update frequency and index-maintenance cost in every repeated-query decision; query count alone is not a preprocessing mandate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_repeated: The heuristic ignores that each update destroys reuse. It becomes valid for static data or when an approved update-aware structure maintains the required query faster.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_updates: This preserves low query latency by returning stale answers, violating correctness. It is legal only if updates are deferred to a new immutable version and queries target the old version explicitly.

items.prompt: Select all conditions that must be checked before repeated queries justify a reusable preprocessing strategy.
constraints: Select all required decision checks.
Query-independent preprocessing is allowed.
Updates and resource limits may exist.

options.text: Future query parameters are unknown, so no query-independent index can be built.
The saved per-query work, multiplied by query count, is large enough to repay setup.
The preprocessed state remains valid or can be maintained within the workload budget.
The statement uses the word repeated, so preprocessing is automatically optimal.
The index fits the permitted memory and preprocessing latency.
The index can answer every allowed query in the query class without knowing each future parameter in advance.

feedback.reason: Amortization, validity lifetime, and resource feasibility jointly determine whether preprocessing is justified. The label 'repeated' is not a complete cost model.

blocks.text: A reusable strategy is justified only when all four gates hold:

items: Compatibility: the index answers the full allowed query class; it need not know future parameter values when its lookup rule is parameter-independent.
Amortization: setup + maintenance + q·indexedQueryCost is no worse than the relevant alternative for the actual workload.
Validity: updates either do not occur or can maintain the index within the operation budget, so answers never use stale state.
Resource fit: construction latency and retained memory stay within their hard limits.

blocks.text: The word repeated supplies only q for the inequality; it proves none of the other gates. The transfer rule is to verify query compatibility, reuse count, index lifetime, and resource fit separately before turning repeated work into preprocessing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.repeated_word: Repeated use is a signal to calculate amortization, not proof of a win. The statement becomes true only after the saved work exceeds setup and maintenance under the resource limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_unknown: Unknown parameters prevent precomputing exact results, but not building a query-independent index. This would block preprocessing only when the index itself depends on knowing all future queries.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.enough_reuse: Without a break-even check, setup may cost more than the work it saves over the actual number of queries.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.state_stays_valid: Without an index-lifetime check, updates can force rebuilds or make answers stale.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.resource_fit: Without resource feasibility, an otherwise attractive index may exceed memory or startup latency.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_class_supported: Without a compatibility check, preprocessing may optimize a related operation while failing some legal query shapes or semantics.

items.prompt: A static array receives one exact membership query, and building a hash set costs O(n) time and O(n) space. Which workload-aware conclusion is strongest?

options.text: Scan the array once unless another contract requires the index; preprocessing cannot repay its setup for this single query.
Build the hash set because expected lookup is O(1), regardless of query count.
Sort first because every query strategy must begin with preprocessing.
Exact membership cannot be answered without a reusable index.

feedback.reason: For one query, index construction is paid once to save at most one scan, so the workload does not justify it by itself.

blocks.text: A direct scan costs O(n) and uses O(1) extra space. Building a hash set adds O(n) setup and memory before the single lookup; it becomes attractive when many queries reuse the same immutable data or when another requirement needs the index. The per-query asymptotic bound alone is not the whole workload cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_hash: Expected O(1) lookup does not erase O(n) setup and space when there is only one query.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_always: Sorting also adds setup and is not required for one exact membership check.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reject_membership: A scan answers one membership query directly; an index is optional, not logically necessary.

items.prompt: A dataset receives frequent point updates and range-sum queries, so rebuilding a prefix array after every update is too expensive. What decision should be evaluated next?

options.text: Compare a data structure with update and query support, such as a dynamic range-sum index, against the actual update/query ratio and resource limits.
Keep using the old prefix array because the query count is high, even when updates make it stale.
Rebuild after every update because preprocessing is always preferable for repeated queries.
Treat updates as irrelevant because range sums are defined on the original dataset.

feedback.reason: Reusable preprocessing is valuable only while its state remains correct within the workload budget; frequent updates shift the comparison to maintenance cost.

blocks.text: A static prefix array gives cheap queries but has O(n) rebuild cost after a point update. A dynamic structure may offer logarithmic updates and queries, but the choice depends on q, update count, memory, and constants. Returning answers from stale state is incorrect, and blindly rebuilding ignores the new workload shape.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_stale_prefix: A stale index violates answer correctness after an update.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rebuild_after_each: Repeated preprocessing can dominate total time when updates are frequent; it must be compared rather than assumed best.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_updates: The update operations change the data on which later queries are defined.

items.prompt: All data is known before execution, but queries arrive one at a time and cannot be batch-reordered. Which strategy property is required?

options.text: Build only query-independent state during preprocessing and ensure each online query can be answered immediately from that state.
Preprocessing is impossible unless every future query parameter is listed before startup.
Sort and reorder queries by value because online arrival order never affects the contract.
Recompute the entire dataset for every query because online inputs forbid reusable state.

feedback.reason: Online arrival constrains response timing, not the ability to build a reusable index from a static dataset.

blocks.text: A prefix table, sorted copy, or hash index can be built before queries arrive when it does not depend on their exact future parameters. Each request then performs its supported lookup immediately. Batch-only transformations are invalid if the service cannot delay or reorder responses, but query-independent preprocessing remains valid.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.know_future_queries: A query-independent index is designed precisely to answer parameters that are not known during construction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.batch_reorder: Reordering violates an online response contract unless the product explicitly permits batching.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rebuild_each_query: Static data is reusable; recomputing it per query discards the purpose of preprocessing.

items.prompt: A direct query costs S, preprocessing costs P, and an indexed query costs Q. Ignoring maintenance, which condition indicates that preprocessing can pay off for m queries?

options.text: P + mQ is no greater than mS, with memory and correctness constraints also satisfied.
Preprocessing is justified whenever P < Q, regardless of m and direct cost.
Compare Q with P only; the number of queries does not affect the decision.
Preprocessing wins whenever m < P because fewer queries reduce total work.

feedback.reason: The workload comparison includes one setup cost and the per-query cost on both sides.

blocks.text: The direct baseline costs mS. The reusable strategy costs P once plus mQ, so the break-even inequality is P + mQ <= mS, subject to the index fitting memory and remaining correct. Maintenance, build latency, expected versus worst-case assumptions, and output costs must be added when present.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_less_q: Preprocessing cost is paid once, while Q is paid m times; comparing only P and Q mixes unlike units.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.q_less_p_only: Query count is exactly what amortizes setup and can reverse the decision.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.m_less_p: A smaller query count generally makes setup harder to repay; the inequality must compare total costs.

items.prompt: A preprocessing structure costs O(n) to build and answers each query in O(1). When can it be a poor choice?
constraints: The input is queried only once.
The build result is not reused elsewhere.

options.text: When the single query does not justify the preprocessing cost compared with a direct O(n) scan.
options.explanation: A one-off workload may be dominated by setup.

options.text: Never; O(1) query time always dominates construction cost.
options.explanation: Total cost includes construction and query count.

options.text: When there are many repeated queries because the structure consumes more memory.
options.explanation: Repeated queries are exactly when build cost can amortize.

options.text: When the input size is small, regardless of latency or memory requirements.
options.explanation: Small inputs do not make all tradeoffs irrelevant.

feedback.reason: Strategy choice must compare total workload cost, not only the per-query asymptotic.

blocks.text: For Q queries, preprocessing total is build(n)+Q*query(n). A direct scan may win for Q=1 or when construction has a large constant, while the indexed structure wins when Q is large enough.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_best: Total cost includes construction and query count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.more_queries_worse: Repeated queries are exactly when build cost can amortize.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_memory: Small inputs do not make all tradeoffs irrelevant.

items.prompt: Why can repeated queries favor a data structure that supports updates even if a static index has faster lookups?
constraints: The underlying input changes between queries.
Answers must reflect the latest state.

options.text: A static index may become stale; update cost must be included so the chosen structure preserves answer correctness over the changing workload.
options.explanation: Fast stale answers are not valid answers.

options.text: Choose the static index because lookup complexity is the only relevant cost.
options.explanation: Updates and freshness are part of the workload contract.

options.text: Rebuild the static index after every query without counting rebuild time.
options.explanation: Rebuild cost can dominate the workload.

options.text: Treat updates as unrelated because queries are still read operations.
options.explanation: Reads over changed data depend on how state is maintained.

feedback.reason: Query volume and mutation frequency jointly determine whether preprocessing remains useful.

blocks.text: A static index is appropriate only when its source assumptions remain true. With updates, include update or rebuild cost and select a representation whose freshness contract is explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lookup_only: Updates and freshness are part of the workload contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rebuild_every_query: Rebuild cost can dominate the workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_mutation: Reads over changed data depend on how state is maintained.

items.prompt: What quantity helps compare a preprocessing strategy against a repeated direct scan?
constraints: Build and query costs can be estimated.
The query count Q is known or bounded.

options.text: Compare buildCost + Q*indexedQueryCost with Q*directQueryCost to find the workload break-even point.
options.explanation: The same number of queries must be charged under both strategies.

options.text: Compare indexedQueryCost with directQueryCost and ignore construction.
options.explanation: Ignoring build cost misprices small workloads.

options.text: Choose the strategy with fewer variables because memory determines all break-even points.
options.explanation: Time and memory are separate constraints.

options.text: The input size alone determines the winner independent of Q.

blocks.text: A preprocessing plan pays its setup once and then answers Q queries. The direct plan pays its scan Q times. The correct comparison can incorporate memory, update, and latency constraints as additional contract terms.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_only: Ignoring build cost misprices small workloads.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memory_only: Time and memory are separate constraints.

items.prompt: When is caching a query result unsafe?
constraints: The answer depends on mutable input state.
The cache key omits part of that state or query contract.

options.text: It is unsafe when the key does not uniquely identify the current input state and query, because a cached answer can be stale or belong to another request.
options.explanation: Caching requires both freshness and key completeness.

options.text: It is always safe if the query text is identical.
options.explanation: Identical text can run against different data or contracts.

options.text: It is safe whenever the result is small because small values cannot become stale.
options.explanation: Result size does not control freshness.

options.text: Any hash key is safe even if collisions are possible.
options.explanation: A collision can return the wrong answer unless handled by a verified key.

feedback.reason: A repeated query is reusable only when its cache identity includes all answer-determining state.

blocks.text: Caching trades computation for a freshness and identity contract. Mutable inputs, omitted parameters, or unchecked hash collisions can make a fast response incorrect.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_query_text: Identical text can run against different data or contracts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.small_result: Result size does not control freshness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_anything: A collision can return the wrong answer unless handled by a verified key.
